# ffimap takes its `-sys` inventory from extern crates alone, so in-crate raw bindings have none

Status: `open`: the change is ffimap `a0797e6` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/`, made on 2026-11-14 at
the user's word, awaiting its review.

Goal: Safety, the unsafe surface's measures; Attribution.

## Signal

A tool that reports what the source contradicts: a campaign whose raw bindings are a module of its crate gets no `fn.ffibox.sys` or `fn.ffibox.wrapper` counters, as though it declared and wrapped no C function.

## Evidence

Found by `ffimap-wrapper-without-alias`'s review-1 on 2026-11-14, reading the driver at ffimap `2a2aa1e`: `count_sys_types` walks `tcx.crates(())`, the extern crates, for those `--sys-crates` names. Since 2026-11-13 this campaign's raw bindings are `crate::sys`, under `sys/<link unit>/`, a module of `libgit2-crustify`, which `--sys-crates` cannot name. glibc-crustify's are a crate, `libc-sys`, and are counted (`fn.ffibox.sys.total` 23). 
Measured on 2026-11-14, on `crustify/devel` at `6d3c7873c`, with the options of the last scan the
dashboard records (`--ffibox --sys-crates libgit2_sys,pcre2_sys`, the regions and seams):

| | 2026-11-10, bindings a crate | 2026-11-14, bindings a module |
|---|---|---|
| `ty.ffibox.sys.total` | 120 | 21 |
| `fn.ffibox.sys.total` | 723 | 222 |
| `fn.ffibox.wrapper.total` | not read | 0 |

What is left is PCRE2's, the one `-sys` crate that is still a crate. The batches since the
bindings moved scanned with `--sys-crates pcre2_sys` and record the same 21 and 222
(`wave-194`, `wave-197`, `wave-225`, `wave-229`, `wave-232`'s `ffimap.json`). The dashboard's
`celled %` cell reads the inventory (`…raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.wrapped` over `….used`), so
for those batches it is taken over PCRE2's types alone, 2 of 5, and its delta reads `+0.00 pp`
whatever the batch did with a libgit2 type.

A second defect came with the same move, and reaches further. The bindings' own code, bindgen's
derives, its `Default` impls and its declarations, is now code of the scanned crate, and
counts as the crate's wherever a counter does not skip a generated file: `ty.ffibox.sys.as`,
which the `C by value` cell reads, went from 111 on 2026-11-10 to 355, with or without the
module named, and `ty.impl_trait`, the `unsafe` counters and `fn.total` rose with it.
The scan is `crustify/tmp/assistant/ffimap-scan/scan.json`.

## Destination

A tool: ffimap's driver and `--sys-crates`, or the `ffimap` tool skill's account of how a campaign with in-crate bindings names them.

## Change

In the driver: an entry of `--sys-crates` written `crate::<path>` names a module of the scanned
crate (`sys_modules`). Its definitions, and those of the modules below it (`in_sys_module`,
which resolves the named modules once), are read as a named crate's items are:

- `count_sys_types` takes them into the inventory, through the same arms as a crate's; and
- every other walk over the crate's definitions and bodies, thirteen of them, `named_defs`
  among them, leaves them out, so that the bindings' own code is not the crate's and does not
  count as a use of the types it declares.

The CLI's help, `README.md`, `docs/analysis.md` and `docs/schema.md` state the form.
The `cells` fixture gains `src/raw.rs` under a feature, bindings as bindgen writes them, and
two tests.

Its other half is one paragraph of Crustify's `ffimap` tool skill, crustify `3dcc464`: a
campaign whose raw bindings are a module of its crate names them to the scan.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--sys-crates` names a module of the scanned crate as `crate::<path>`: its raw bindings join the `-sys` inventory and leave every other counter, and the `ffimap` skill has a scan name them | `libgit2-crustify`, `ffimap-sys-inventory-in-crate` | ffimap `a0797e6`; crustify `3dcc464` | once this campaign's raw bindings became a module of its crate, its scans read PCRE2's inventory alone and counted the bindings' own code as the crate's, so `celled %` and `C by value` measured nothing of its batches | a scan whose `ty.ffibox.sys.total` or `fn.ffibox.sys.total` falls by an order of magnitude from the scan before it with no binding removed; a counter with a site inside a generated bindings file; or a campaign whose bindings are a module scanning without naming it | watched |

## Validation

- ffimap's suite, in its own checkout, outside any Cargo workspace: 147 tests pass. Two are new.
  One expects, with `crate::raw` named, one more C type behind a pointer, two more functions
  and one more wrapper, and no other inventory or wrapper counter moved, `used` included. The
  other expects that the module's code counts as the crate's while unnamed, that named, no
  counter but the inventory's has a site in it, and that every counter then reads what the
  crate reads without the module. The 21 other driver tests are unchanged.
- On real code, libgit2-crustify at `6d3c7873c`, the campaign's options:

  | | 2026-11-10, bindings a crate | bindings a module, old driver | new driver, `crate::sys` named |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `ty.ffibox.sys.total` | 120 | 21 | 128 |
  | `…raw_ptr_in_sys.total` | 115 | 21 | 122 |
  | `…raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.used` | 78 | 5 | 85 |
  | `…raw_ptr_in_sys.of_which.wrapped` | 70 | 2 | 77 |
  | `ty.ffibox.sys.as.total` | 111 | 355 | 122 |
  | `ty.ffibox.sys.as.by_val.total` | 111 | 219 | 119 |
  | `fn.ffibox.sys.total` | 723 | 222 | 785 |
  | `fn.ffibox.sys.of_which.used` | 452 | 6 | 509 |
  | `fn.ffibox.wrapper.total` | 511 | 0 | 590 |

  84 of 767 values move against the old driver: the inventory's, the wrapper counters', and the
  counters the bindings' own code had inflated. `celled %` reads 77 of 85, where 2026-11-10
  read 70 of 78. The scans are `crustify/tmp/assistant/ffimap-scan/scan.json` (old driver) and
  `scan-new2.json`; `scan-new.json` is review-1's commit, which read 106 used.

## Review

`review-1` (Opus 5.5, `$2.63`), on ffimap `8cd7a26`: **rejected**, four fixes required; it weakens no
check. A named crate was unchanged, the module walk took the right items, and the totals
checked against the bindings. The fixes, made as `a0797e6`: (1) the bindings' own declarations
counted as uses of their types, so `used` read 106 and `celled %` a wrong ratio; (2) the
bindings' own code counts as the crate's, a second signal, which the change now answers by
having a named module leave every other counter; (3) this proposal's evidence was wrong about
`C by value`, which does not read the inventory; (4) no run would name the module unless the
`ffimap` skill says so, which crustify `3dcc464` adds. Its sturdier matching of the module is
taken too.

# Goals

ffimap measures how a Rust crate meets C: what its code leaves unsafe, which
raw pointers it hands to its consumers, what it claims about memory and threads
that no type system checked, how it reaches C and how C reaches it, and how much
of that it says through a convention such as ffibox's. Each measure is a fact
the compiler states, so that a person or an agent can check a change to the
crate against the crate before it, and see where the change moved what.

Three parties use it:

- **the driver** states facts: a rustc pass over one build's HIR and type
  information;
- **inputs** state what a fact cannot: the names that need judgement or a
  convention, which the caller passes (`--sys-crates`, `--seams`, `--regions`,
  `--barriers`, `--ffibox`);
- **readers** take the measures: a reviewer forming suspicions, an agent
  verifying its own change, a dashboard tracking a campaign. They read a
  document, or the difference between two.

The goals below are grouped by what they serve. Each states what it means and
how it is checked. A change that departs from one says so, in its commit and
here.

## Facts

### G1. Facts, not data flow

Every counter is a declaration or one expression node, read after macro
expansion, `cfg` selection and type resolution. Nothing follows a value through
locals, memory or calls, and no points-to analysis runs. Where an answer would
need data flow, ffimap counts the fact it can see at the site and leaves the
rest to a reader, who has the sites to start from.

*Checked by:* every counter's row in [`schema.md`](schema.md) names the one
declaration or node that moves it, and [`analysis.md`](analysis.md) the rule it
is decided by.

### G2. Compiler-precise

A fact comes from the compiler's own resolution, never from source text: a
callee is identified by its definition, a type by its `DefId`, an ABI by the
signature's. A name is matched only where the compiler cannot say more, and
only against a caller's input or a fixed vocabulary.

*Checked by:* the driver reads names only in the tables
[`analysis.md`](analysis.md) lists.

### G3. One build, stated

The facts are those of the build `cargo check --all-targets` compiles on the
pinned toolchain. What that build does not compile contributes nothing, and a
crate that does not build has no counts rather than approximate ones.

*Checked by:* [`analysis.md`](analysis.md#3-the-build) describes the build,
and `counts_unavailable` carries the reason a document has none.

## Measures

### G4. Measures of how the crate meets C

Each counter bears on one of four properties, which its row says: safety (how
much is left unsafe, and where), soundness (claims and conversions a reviewer
must vouch for), ergonomics (what a consumer has to handle that C would have
made it handle) and idiomaticity (how much of the API speaks Rust's own
vocabulary). A counter that bears on none is not added.

*Checked by:* the readings of [`schema.md`](schema.md#31-the-readings-worth-taking)
name the counters each property is read from.

### G5. Feedback through differences and sites

A reader learns most from two documents of one crate: which counters a change
moved, and, with sites, where the new increments are. `ffimap diff` states
that difference, so that an agent checks its own change without reading the
whole document.

*Checked by:* the diff of a document against itself is empty, and the diff of
two scans of the canary differs in exactly the items changed between them.

### G6. No target values

A lower count is not a better crate, as
[`schema.md`](schema.md#33-no-target-values) explains. ffimap states figures,
and a threshold is its reader's to set.

## Inputs

### G7. Judgement is an input, never a guess

What needs judgement or a convention to decide enters as a flag the caller
sets: the crates that are C's, the functions that are seams, the modules that
are regions, the convention a crate is built on. ffimap does not discover them,
and a counter that needs one is absent without it rather than zero.

*Checked by:* every such counter is registered only under its flag, which
`RegistryTests` holds.

### G8. General rules, no overfitting

A rule follows from Rust's and C's semantics and holds for every crate. It
matches no names, paths or conventions of one crate or one tool that builds
crates, and does not special-case the crate that motivated it. A convention's
vocabulary, such as ffibox's, is a fixed set of arms its flag turns on, read
from the convention's own declarations.

*Checked by:* each rule has a fixture written for it, and its effect is
measured on a crate other than the one that motivated it (G10).

## Validation

### G9. Every counter is tested

Each counter has a fixture whose expected count is derived by hand, item by
item, with the items that must NOT move it beside those that must. Every site a
counter records is checked to be addressable and to sum to the counter.

*Checked by:* the canary, cells and interop suites, and `SiteTests`.

### G10. Every change is measured on real code

A change to a counter is run on the crates under [`examples/`](../examples)
before it lands, and its commit states what moved and that nothing else did.
An unexplained difference is a defect until it is explained.

*Checked by:* the commit message, and the rescanned examples.

### G11. Readings are checked against the source

A new counter's sites are read on at least one real crate, to show that what it
counts is what its row says it counts.

*Checked by:* the commit message names the crate and what its sites showed.

## Interface

### G12. Deterministic

The same tree under the same scanner gives the same bytes. The document
records the scanner and its inputs, so a difference between two documents can
be told from a difference between two scanners.

*Checked by:* the `scanner` field, and the canary scanned twice.

### G13. Documented

Every counter has a row, every input a description, and every known blind spot
an entry in [`analysis.md`](analysis.md#12-what-the-analysis-cannot-see) or
[`TODO.md`](TODO.md).

*Checked by:* `SchemaDocTests`, both ways.

## Non-goals

- **Data flow and points-to analysis.** See G1.
- **Proving soundness.** ffimap measures where a reviewer should look; the
  reviewer decides what is wrong.
- **Lints.** What rustc and Clippy already check is theirs.
- **Target values.** See G6.
- **The C side.** What the C does with what it is given is the C analysis's.

## Known departures

- `code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export` attributes a block to the C-ABI
  boundary by its function's ABI and symbol, and so stays without `--regions`;
  its name is a campaign's term for that boundary rather than Rust's (G8).
- The `--ffibox` arms match the `as_ref` and `as_mut` layout accessors by name,
  which holds only where the convention does (G2).
- `ffimap api` reads rustdoc JSON instead of the driver's build (G3), and keys
  on crustify's anchor convention, whose grammar and kind table it fixes
  ([`api.md`](api.md#2-c-items-and-their-stand-ins)) (G8). A crate without the
  anchors has only unattributed surface.

must vouch for), ergonomics (what a consumer has to handle that C would have
made it handle) and idiomaticity (how much of the API speaks Rust's own
vocabulary). A counter that bears on none is not added.

*Checked by:* the readings of [`schema.md`](schema.md#31-the-readings-worth-taking)
name the counters each property is read from.

### G5. Feedback through differences and sites

A reader learns most from two documents of one crate: which counters a change
moved, and, with sites, where the new increments are. `ffimap diff` states
that difference, so that an agent checks its own change without reading the
whole document.

*Checked by:* the diff of a document against itself is empty, and the diff of
two scans of the canary differs in exactly the items changed between them.

### G6. No target values

A lower count is not a better crate, as
[`schema.md`](schema.md#33-no-target-values) explains. ffimap states figures,
and a threshold is its reader's to set.

## Inputs

### G7. Judgement is an input, never a guess

What needs judgement or a convention to decide enters as a flag the caller
sets: the crates that are C's, the functions that are seams, the modules that
are regions, the convention a crate is built on. ffimap does not discover them,
and a counter that needs one is absent without it rather than zero.

*Checked by:* every such counter is registered only under its flag, which
`RegistryTests` holds.

### G8. General rules, no overfitting

A rule follows from Rust's and C's semantics and holds for every crate. It
matches no names, paths or conventions of one crate or one tool that builds
crates, and does not special-case the crate that motivated it. A convention's
vocabulary, such as ffibox's, is a fixed set of arms its flag turns on, read
from the convention's own declarations.

*Checked by:* each rule has a fixture written for it, and its effect is
measured on a crate other than the one that motivated it (G10).

## Validation

### G9. Every counter is tested

Each counter has a fixture whose expected count is derived by hand, item by
item, with the items that must NOT move it beside those that must. Every site a
counter records is checked to be addressable and to sum to the counter.

*Checked by:* the canary, cells and interop suites, and `SiteTests`.

### G10. Every change is measured on real code

A change to a counter is run on the crates under [`examples/`](../examples)
before it lands, and its commit states what moved and that nothing else did.
An unexplained difference is a defect until it is explained.

*Checked by:* the commit message, and the rescanned examples.

### G11. Readings are checked against the source

A new counter's sites are read on at least one real crate, to show that what it
counts is what its row says it counts.

*Checked by:* the commit message names the crate and what its sites showed.

## Interface

### G12. Deterministic

The same tree under the same scanner gives the same bytes. The document
records the scanner and its inputs, so a difference between two documents can
be told from a difference between two scanners.

*Checked by:* the `scanner` field, and the canary scanned twice.

### G13. Documented

Every counter has a row, every input a description, and every known blind spot
an entry in [`analysis.md`](analysis.md#12-what-the-analysis-cannot-see) or
[`TODO.md`](TODO.md).

*Checked by:* `SchemaDocTests`, both ways.

## Non-goals

- **Data flow and points-to analysis.** See G1.
- **Proving soundness.** ffimap measures where a reviewer should look; the
  reviewer decides what is wrong.
- **Lints.** What rustc and Clippy already check is theirs.
- **Target values.** See G6.
- **The C side.** What the C does with what it is given is the C analysis's.

## Known departures

- `code.unsafe_block.of_which.ffi_export` attributes a block to the C-ABI
  boundary by its function's ABI and symbol, and so stays without `--regions`;
  its name is a campaign's term for that boundary rather than Rust's (G8).

  which holds only where the convention does (G2).

  on crustify's anchor convention, whose grammar and kind table it fixes
  ([`api.md`](api.md#2-c-items-and-their-stand-ins)) (G8). A crate without the
  anchors has only unattributed surface.

# Lessons

Rules that hold for this campaign's target alone, each with the evidence it rests on and
its scope, as the `evolution` skill's Lessons section describes. Every run reads them
before its first step.

## Before `git_libgit2_init`, probe libgit2's allocator only through a release

**Rule.** Before `git_libgit2_init`, `git__allocator` is the failing family
(`src/util/allocators/failalloc.c`), and a test may reach it only through a release:
`git_odb_backend_data_free`, which is `git__free`, sets no error. Any allocation then
fails, and `git__malloc`, `git__realloc` and every error setter report through
`git_error_set_oom` or `set_error`, whose thread-state lookup reads TLS key 0 before
`git_error_global_init` has created libgit2's key: it may return another component's
slot and write `&oom_error` into it. The same holds for an allocator installed with
`set_allocator` before initialisation that fails a request.

**Evidence.** `git_odb_backend_data_alloc`'s finding in the ownership store (ASan
unknown-crash in `git_error_set_oom`, `errors.c:170`); `src/util/errors.c`'s
`threadstate_get`; the equivalence test of `wave-176/batch-0`
(`tests/equiv/src/util/allocators/failalloc.rs`), which compares the C release with the
Rust family's and leaves `malloc` and `realloc` uncompared for this reason. The family's
routines called directly, as `git_failalloc_malloc` through its raw binding, set no error
and are outside the rule: `wave-176/batch-1` compares them so in the test process.

**Scope.** The tests of `src/util/allocators/*.c`, `src/util/alloc.c` and
`src/util/errors.c`, and any test that runs libgit2 before its initialisation.

## libgit2's allocator family is reached through `alloc.rs`'s strategies

- **Rule.** Rust allocates, copies and releases memory in libgit2's allocator family
  (`git__malloc`, `git__calloc`, `git__mallocarray`, `git__strdup`, `git__strndup`,
  `git__substrdup`, `git__free`) through the strategies of `src/libgit2/src/util/alloc.rs`:
  `Free` / `AllocBox`, `ArrayFree` / `AllocVec` and `StrFree` / `AllocStr`, which call
  those primitives through their raw bindings, the two `static inline` ones through the
  wrappers in `sys/libgit2/static_fns.c`. New owners of memory libgit2 frees with
  `git__free` use those policies, not new ones over `git_odb_backend_data_alloc` /
  `git_odb_backend_data_free`, whose bodies are `git__malloc` / `git__free` but which are
  odb.c's exports and loop back through the strategies once odb.c is ported.
- **Evidence.** wave 12 batch 1 (`src/util/alloc.c`) reached the family through odb.c's
  exports while the primitives were hidden in `libgit2.so`; the static campaign link
  (`d21c78c70`) made them link, and wave 12 batch 2 rebound the strategies over them. The
  `OdbData*` policies of `src/libgit2/src/libgit2/odb.rs` (`OdbDataBox`, `OdbDataVec`,
  `OdbDataStr`, `OdbDataStrVec`) and the raw `git_odb_backend_data_alloc` calls of
  `oidarray.rs` predate them.
- **Scope.** Every module's owners of strings, singletons and arrays libgit2 frees with
  `git__free`. The existing `OdbData*` uses are odb.c's batches' to revisit: where they
  hold memory C frees with `git__free` rather than with `git_odb_backend_data_free`, they
  take these strategies.

## libgit2's allocator storage is 8-aligned, not `malloc`-aligned

- **Rule.** A policy over libgit2's allocator family (`git__malloc` and its siblings, and the
  exports whose bodies are theirs, such as `git_odb_backend_data_alloc`) vouches for the
  wider of `usize`'s and `u64`'s alignment, never `max_align_t`'s. libgit2 configured with
  `DEBUG_STRICT_ALLOC`, as its own CI is, runs on `debugalloc`, which returns `malloc`'s block
  offset by a `size_t`. A type aligned to 16 is refused at compile time, not allocated.
- **Evidence.** wave 12 batch 3's `ub_safe/strict-alloc-misaligns-wide-runs`: with
  `MAX_ALIGN = align_of::<max_align_t>()`, `AllocVec::<u128>::from_slice` formed a misaligned
  slice from safe code on a private `-DDEBUG_STRICT_ALLOC=ON` build. `odb.rs`'s `DATA_ALIGN`
  already followed this rule.
- **Scope.** Every lifecycle policy, owner or alignment claim over storage libgit2's
  allocator makes, whether it comes from Rust or from C.

## The tree's inline `mod unit_tests` modules are no precedent for test placement

- **Rule.** A new unit test of a module's public interface goes in `tests/unit_pub`, at the
  tested TU's path (`tests/unit_pub/src/util/...`), and one of an internal routine in an
  inline `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside it, as the conventions' Testing section places
  them, whatever the module's file or its neighbours hold. The 34 inline `mod unit_tests`
  modules under `src/` (`alloc.rs` and `errors.rs` among them) predate that placement and
  mix both kinds; a batch that adds tests to one of those files puts its new tests where the
  conventions place them, and leaves the old ones to the batches that port their modules.
  Until `tests/unit_pub` reaches the working branch, a wave that needs it creates it with
  the same `main.rs`, `src.rs`, directory files and `[[test]] unit_pub` entry as waves 169
  and 176, so that the branches merge with only the one-line `mod` additions conflicting.
- **Evidence.** wave 182 batch 0 (`cff595a09`) put `win32_leakcheck.rs`'s three
  public-interface tests in an inline `mod unit_tests`, following `alloc.rs` and
  `errors.rs`; its module pass (`wave-182/batch-1`) moved them to `tests/unit_pub` and
  renamed the module `unit_priv` (a `conventions` finding).

- **Rule.** A new unit test of a module's public interface goes in `tests/unit_pub`, at the
  tested TU's path (`tests/unit_pub/src/util/...`), and one of an internal routine in an
  inline `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside it, as the conventions' Testing section places
  them, whatever the module's file or its neighbours hold. The 34 inline `mod unit_tests`
  modules under `src/` (`alloc.rs` and `errors.rs` among them) predate that placement and
  mix both kinds; a batch that adds tests to one of those files puts its new tests where the
  conventions place them, and leaves the old ones to the batches that port their modules.
  Until `tests/unit_pub` reaches the working branch, a wave that needs it creates it with
  the same `main.rs`, `src.rs`, directory files and `[[test]] unit_pub` entry as waves 169
  and 176, so that the branches merge with only the one-line `mod` additions conflicting.
- **Evidence.** wave 182 batch 0 (`cff595a09`) put `win32_leakcheck.rs`'s three
  public-interface tests in an inline `mod unit_tests`, following `alloc.rs` and
  `errors.rs`; its module pass (`wave-182/batch-1`) moved them to `tests/unit_pub` and
  renamed the module `unit_priv` (a `conventions` finding).

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

content.content:
---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Worksets

The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build
configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives.
A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source.

For `ub`, the modules that hold the smells ffimap's review guidance lists for `ub` are
reviewed first, in that order; for `contracts`, those that hold the crate's unsafe API and
its justifications, the `contracts` counters above. The rest of the crate
follows the smells.

The modules are batched by their sites, and a module that is split keeps a type, trait
impl or function with its sites in one batch. A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`,

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.
